biggest_blockers.title: topology-vpc-unproven
biggest_blockers.detail: The project can be taken as one VPC's boundary only if every resource that names a VPC provably names the estate's one, and this estate does not show it: the VPC this security group names, or the VPC another resource of the estate names (a network ACL, a flow log, a peering connection, a Cloud Control subnet, ...), is a literal id, a variable, a data source, an attribute of a VPC other than its id (its arn, its owner id, ...) or an expression the scan cannot reduce to one reference to the VPC the estate creates (or the estate creates no VPC of its own). A unit placed in a subnet that the scan cannot show is one of the estate's (a server, load balancer, function or NAT gateway in a subnet given by a variable, a data source or a literal id) is in the same position: it may stand in another VPC. The draft puts every network, security group and routing table in the one var.project_id and cannot say that they all belong to one VPC. Confirm which VPC each of them is in, and whether the networks of another VPC belong in this project or in a project of their own joined through a Network Area. No unit of the VPC topology is automation-eligible until then (gate blocker TOPOLOGY:vpc-unproven).

biggest_blockers.title: sg-egress-restricted
biggest_blockers.detail: The source restricts egress (the AWS provider removes AWS's default allow-all egress rule; only the listed egress rules apply). Every new STACKIT security group gets two default egress rules, IPv4 and IPv6, with no ip range (any address), no protocol and no port restriction (the test of 2026-10-07, 2026-10-07: API read-back of a new group, docs concepts page), that stackit_security_group (the pinned STACKIT provider) does not manage — as generated, the draft allows all egress. After apply, delete them (stackit security-group rule list / delete --security-group-id <id>), or egress is wider than in the source.

biggest_blockers.title: sg-rule-not-rendered
biggest_blockers.detail: At least one rule of this group is not in the draft as the source has it. The plan withholds it, holds it as a commented-out rule until a value or a decision is filled in, writes it with a fact that decides what it allows not carried exactly, or cannot name it at all because the source has more rules than are visible statically (a dynamic block over a collection, a count or a rule list that is not known until apply, or a list with a hidden member: the plan's INCOMPLETE action says which set and why, the draft's TODO "rules beyond the known set" names it, and only the known rules are drafted). Typical causes: a protocol, port or source whose value is known only at apply time or comes from a root variable; a source group that is a choice between groups or not a group of the draft; a protocol with no STACKIT counterpart; an ICMP type with every code; an ICMP or ICMPv6 rule whose range is of the other IP family (the API answers HTTP 400, the test of 2026-10-08); a tcp or udp rule with a negative port, a port above 65535, a reversed range, or port 0 only (STACKIT stores no port range for 0 to 0, so the rule would match every port). A tcp or udp range that starts at port 0 and ends below 65535 is written from port 1 (the STACKIT API rejects a range that starts at 0; tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-07): port 0 itself is not carried. A stackit_security_group_rule without protocol, port_range or source allows everything (the pinned STACKIT provider), so such a rule is never widened; re-create it with the values it needs (the plan names each one).

options.title: Export the data from the source and import it with the clients of the target engine
options.effect: A person exports the data from the source and imports it into the STACKIT instance with the clients of its engine during a window the business accepts, then checks that the copy is complete; the clients reach the instance at the host and port its credential states. The source and the target engine may differ (DynamoDB to MongoDB Flex), so the export is converted where they do. The plan holds the steps of this option as typed steps: for a PostgreSQL database, for a MySQL, MariaDB or Aurora MySQL database moving to MariaDB and for an RDS for SQL Server database moving to SQLServer Flex (the native backup, its copy to a STACKIT S3 bucket and the import_database call) the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the dump or backup and the restore or import inside it, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an ElastiCache, MemoryDB or ElastiCache serverless cache moving to a Key Value Store the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy by a client, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster moving to PostgreSQL Flex the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy of the tables by a client (the schema from the catalogs of the cluster, or from pg_dump --schema-only where the preflight shows that it works, and the rows through the PostgreSQL protocol: no AWS page read documents a dump of a cluster), the reconcile and the cleanup; for an OpenSearch store the write freeze, the copy and the reconcile. The decision offers this option only for a store whose STACKIT service documents a way in with such clients: PostgreSQL Flex (for an Aurora DSQL cluster, which has no change stream, this option and the tool of the customer's own are the only ones; the replication of the engine is not offered), MariaDB (the mysql client loads a dump into an empty instance), SQLServer Flex (a .bak file imported with import_database), Key Value Store (the tutorial migrates a Redis instance by the MIGRATE command; for an ElastiCache source, where AWS lists migrate among the commands unavailable for caches running Redis OSS, the copy is a client that iterates the keys with SCAN and copies each with DUMP, PTTL and RESTORE; for a MemoryDB source, where AWS lists migrate, sync, psync, bgsave, save and config among the unavailable commands and the cluster mode is always on, the same client copy runs against every shard primary found with CLUSTER NODES or CLUSTER SLOTS, with TLS where the source has it and an ACL user that reaches every key; whether DUMP, RESTORE and PTTL run on a standard MemoryDB cluster is not stated by AWS, and for a member of a multi-Region cluster, whose page lists PTTL as unsupported, the step says the TTLs are not carried) and OpenSearch (the reindex operation). For a store without a documented way in (MongoDB Flex, a memcached cache) it is not offered and the decision offers the tool of the customer's own alone.

options.title: Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover
options.effect: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). The source needs a change and a reboot to turn replication on, and the target must be able to reach the source. Inside the write freeze the person waits until the target has caught up, compares both sides and switches the clients, then removes the replication. For a PostgreSQL database the plan holds the steps of this option (the initial copy, the watch of the lag, the freeze, the final copy, the reconcile and the cleanup); for an S3 bucket this option is not available, because S3 Replication copies between Amazon S3 buckets and no STACKIT bucket is documented as a destination (the plan holds the two copy tools instead); for any other engine this option is not offered, because no STACKIT service other than PostgreSQL Flex documents the replication of a source engine into it (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch and MongoDB Flex document none, and the SQLServer Flex page on transactional replication describes an on-premises publisher and does not name Amazon RDS as one), so the decision of such a store offers the export and the import with the engine clients where its service documents them, and the tool of the customer's own.

The plan holds the steps of this option as typed steps: for a PostgreSQL database, for a MySQL, MariaDB or Aurora MySQL database moving to MariaDB and for an RDS for SQL Server database moving to SQLServer Flex (the native backup, its copy to a STACKIT S3 bucket and the import_database call) the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the dump or backup and the restore or import inside it, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an ElastiCache, MemoryDB or ElastiCache serverless cache moving to a Key Value Store the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy by a client, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster moving to PostgreSQL Flex the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy of the tables by a client (the schema from the catalogs of the cluster, or from pg_dump --schema-only where the preflight shows that it works, and the rows through the PostgreSQL protocol: no AWS page read documents a dump of a cluster), the reconcile and the cleanup; for an OpenSearch store the write freeze, the copy and the reconcile. The decision offers this option only for a store whose STACKIT service documents a way in with such clients: PostgreSQL Flex (for an Aurora DSQL cluster, which has no change stream, this option and the tool of the customer's own are the only ones; the replication of the engine is not offered), MariaDB (the mysql client loads a dump into an empty instance), SQLServer Flex (a .bak file imported with import_database), Key Value Store (the tutorial migrates a Redis instance by the MIGRATE command; for an ElastiCache source, where AWS lists migrate among the commands unavailable for caches running Redis OSS, the copy is a client that iterates the keys with SCAN and copies each with DUMP, PTTL and RESTORE; for a MemoryDB source, where AWS lists migrate, sync, psync, bgsave, save and config among the unavailable commands and the cluster mode is always on, the same client copy runs against every shard primary found with CLUSTER NODES or CLUSTER SLOTS, with TLS where the source has it and an ACL user that reaches every key; whether DUMP, RESTORE and PTTL run on a standard MemoryDB cluster is not stated by AWS, and for a member of a multi-Region cluster, whose page lists PTTL as unsupported, the step says the TTLs are not carried) and OpenSearch (the reindex operation). For a store without a documented way in (MongoDB Flex, a memcached cache) it is not offered and the decision offers the tool of the customer's own alone.

resolution_paths.title: Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover
effects: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). The source needs a change and a reboot to turn replication on, and the target must be able to reach the source. Inside the write freeze the person waits until the target has caught up, compares both sides and switches the clients, then removes the replication. For a PostgreSQL database the plan holds the steps of this option (the initial copy, the watch of the lag, the freeze, the final copy, the reconcile and the cleanup); for an S3 bucket this option is not available, because S3 Replication copies between Amazon S3 buckets and no STACKIT bucket is documented as a destination (the plan holds the two copy tools instead); for any other engine this option is not offered, because no STACKIT service other than PostgreSQL Flex documents the replication of a source engine into it (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch and MongoDB Flex document none, and the SQLServer Flex page on transactional replication describes an on-premises publisher and does not name Amazon RDS as one), so the decision of such a store offers the export and the import with the engine clients where its service documents them, and the tool of the customer's own.

options.title: Accept the public endpoint, limited by its access list
options.effect: The endpoint the draft writes is applied as written: the instance (or the Kubernetes API) is reached at its public address, and only the IP networks of its access list may connect (acl of stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance, sgw_acl of stackit_mariadb_instance, extensions.acl.allowed_cidrs of stackit_ske_cluster; parameters.sgw_acl of stackit_valkey_instance (Key Value Store), stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance and stackit_redis_instance, a comma-separated list of IP networks in CIDR notation, left to the default when the draft states none). The exposure is wider than the source's and the difference is accepted. Maturity: for stackit_ske_cluster this is the ACL-restricted public control plane: GA, not the source's private endpoint (the ACL how-to, last updated Aug 19, 2026, carries no Private Preview or beta notice, and says ACLs only control access to the API of the public control plane); the provider documents acl and sgw_acl of the data services without a preview notice. For an Application Load Balancer: it is created with the access control the draft writes, options.access_control.allowed_source_ranges, one set of source ranges for the whole load balancer (or none, where the draft can prove no range), so it admits more clients than the source's security groups; the restriction the set cannot express is the client-access manual step of the plan behind this decision, which follows the load balancer. The draft carries this option out BY DEFAULT for the Kubernetes API of a cluster whose source endpoint is private (stackit_ske_cluster, extensions.acl): of the three options it is the only one that is production grade (the ACL-restricted public control plane is GA, the network-area-only control plane is a Private Preview on request, not recommended for production, and cannot be combined with the ACL extension) and it is fail-closed, because only the CIDRs of the access list may connect. The decision stays OPEN with this option marked DEFAULT; the access list stays a required variable with no default (no CIDR is invented, and neither the cluster's own egress addresses nor a STACKIT range is a fallback, because the source's private clients are the admin and CI networks only the customer knows) that refuses an empty list, so the step of the cluster waits for the networks the person lists and not for the decision. The draft carries it out by default for a managed data service (stackit_postgresflex_instance, stackit_sqlserverflex_instance, stackit_mariadb_instance, stackit_mongodbflex_instance, stackit_valkey_instance, stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance, stackit_redis_instance) as well, on the same grounds and only when all of these hold: the decision is open and no review declines it; the access list the block writes (acl, sgw_acl) is one variable the draft wrote, of type list(string), with no default, that refuses an empty list, an empty entry and null; and the draft could not derive the clients' addresses (where every client is a drafted cluster or a drafted server with a public address the access list already has those addresses as its default, and the decision stands on that default). Of the options, accept-the-public-endpoint is the only one that is generally available for every data service (the network-area-only scope is a Private Preview for enabled accounts and exists for PostgreSQL Flex and SQL Server Flex only), and with a required, non-empty list it is fail-closed: only the CIDRs the person lists may connect. No CIDR is invented, and STACKIT's documented service ranges are no fallback. The default applies to a source that is private and to one whose exposure cannot be read, because the draft writes the same fail-closed endpoint for both. The access-scope variable of PostgreSQL Flex and SQL Server Flex keeps no default, and the critical network exposure of the unit stays open for the assurance until a review that chooses this option also states an exposure_acceptance (its statement and scope), which records the public endpoint as an accepted design change naming the reviewer, never as an equivalent. A review that names another option for the record, or rejects the proposal, declines the default. A cluster whose source endpoint is public gets no decision: its public_access_cidrs are the access list.

options.effect: The draft already writes the derived plan, flavor or machine type (as the default of the variable for a plan or a machine type, as the literal of the block for a database flavor), said as DEFAULT on the block: the instance or the pool is created with it and the cost page prices it. Confirming it accepts the proposal as the starting size of the target; it does not say that the size carries the load, which the source does not state, and the disk of a plan is the smallest of that size. The memory was compared in bytes: the API states the memory of a PostgreSQL Flex and a SQL Server Flex flavor in Gibibyte, the unit of the source; the plan tables of Key Value Store and RabbitMQ and the MongoDB Flex flavors state their RAM as GB without defining it, so the draft took the plan or flavor that holds the source's memory when a GB is 10^9 bytes (it then holds it when a GB is 2^30 bytes as well) and says where that made it larger than the reading of a GB as a GiB; a machine type's memory is the catalogue's ram_mb read as MiB, an inference the API does not state. The next run writes the same default.

options.title: Place the cluster and the servers in one STACKIT network, and admit the clients of the managed services by access lists naming its range
options.effect: The Kubernetes cluster is deployed into one network (network.id of stackit_ske_cluster names a STACKIT Network Area network; a node pool states no network, so the tasks the source spread over several subnets share it), the servers are placed in it by their network interfaces (network_id of stackit_network_interface), and a managed database or cache is not placed in a network: its access list (acl of stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_mongodbflex_instance) names the range of that network. The other drafted networks of the subnets hold none of these consumers. The draft writes the cluster half of this option by default (network = { id = ... } on the drafted stackit_ske_cluster, marked DEFAULT) where the target project is not stated to be outside a Network Area, the draft asks for no such project, the cluster serves workloads of exactly one drafted network, and every other consumer of that network has a decision of its own; where one of these does not hold it writes no network.id and a person carries the cluster half out. The access lists of the managed services are a separate default of the draft and not written by this option: a person (or that default) carries the services half out, and the network's step stays held until the decision is answered where the draft binds nothing.

effects: The draft writes the database user (stackit_postgresflex_user, stackit_sqlserverflex_user, stackit_mariadb_credential or stackit_mongodbflex_user) and STACKIT generates its password at the apply. The source password and its Secrets Manager management are not copied and the clients get new credentials: after the apply a person reads the output, puts it into the connection settings of every client (a cutover action) and keeps it in the secret store the customer uses. This is the default the draft writes. A review records the choice; the new credentials reaching the clients stays the manual work of the record.

resolution.source_observation: The plan writes no resource for module.vpc.module.vpc.aws_route_table.private: STACKIT's default routing replaces the table, with a loss: a route of the table sends traffic to a NAT gateway (the others, if any, to an internet gateway), and the reachability is observed on the target for a project outside a Network Area, which this draft does not write. Observed in one sandbox project outside a Network Area (tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-10; routing tables are refused there): a routed network reaches the internet with no route and no routing table configured, a server without a public IP through the network's shared SNAT address and a server with a public IP through its own; nothing initiated from the internet reached a server behind the network address; egress is restricted by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route; routed networks reach each other with no table. No stackit_routing_table is drafted. A NAT gateway adds what an internet route does not. Its fixed egress address is LOST (observed): the address a routed STACKIT network leaves by is the network's publicIp, one address for every routed network of the project, not fixed (it changed twice when every network of the project was deleted) and not settable (a PATCH of it answers 202 and is ignored), so a third party's allow-list on the NAT gateway's address does not survive; a STACKIT public IP per server keeps its address, the only one the probe saw stay fixed. The egress restriction (the gateway as the only way out of a private subnet) is carried by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route (observed); whether the source restricts egress that way is for the architect. The absence of inbound paths of a private subnet is observed for a server without a public IP (tcp 22, 80 and 8080 on the network address). Not observed: a Network Area and its default routing table. The outbound address of the servers an allow-list names is the architect's choice: keep the changing address, or give each server that an allow-list names a STACKIT public IP. The plan writes no resource for module.vpc.module.vpc.aws_route_table.public: STACKIT's default routing replaces the table: every route of the table sends traffic to an internet gateway, and the equivalence is observed on the target for a project outside a Network Area, which this draft does not write. Observed in one sandbox project outside a Network Area (tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-10; routing tables are refused there): a routed network reaches the internet with no route and no routing table configured, a server without a public IP through the network's shared SNAT address and a server with a public IP through its own; nothing initiated from the internet reached a server behind the network address; egress is restricted by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route; routed networks reach each other with no table. No stackit_routing_table is drafted. Observed in one project of one region on one day, so not HIGH; not observed: a Network Area and its default routing table, where this would be open again. The draft writes no routing table for a table whose routes all send traffic to an internet gateway: STACKIT's default routing gave a routed network the same reachability in one STACKIT test project outside a Network Area. The default routing table of a Network Area was never read.

proposed.reason: Suggested from the workloads of the source, not confirmed by the customer: these groups are a reading of names, tags and references in the Terraform. Nothing is an application until the applications file (--applications) or the review file states it, and where it does the stated applications win and the suggestion is shown as a diff against them.
proposed.rule: One group per workload that is switched on: an ECS service, a Lambda function, a Kubernetes deployment, stateful set, daemon set, replication controller, pod, job or cron job, a load balancer with the instances and Auto Scaling groups it routes to, an instance or Auto Scaling group no load balancer fronts, or an EKS cluster when the estate holds no Kubernetes workload (such a group is a platform: its workloads are not visible in Terraform). A group holds its workload and the datastores, security groups, roles, log groups, secrets, keys and similar units that only that workload reaches: what the workload depends on (for an ECS service what its task definition names, for a Lambda function what its environment names, for a load balancer what it routes to), what those depend on in turn, the queues, streams, topics, buckets and EventBridge rules that feed a member (an event source mapping, a subscription, a rule target or the permission that names the rule, a bucket notification), the units a policy of a member names in a statement that is not a Deny, the units a DNS record that the workload names points at (a DNS record or a service-discovery registration that only points at a member is shown and adds no member), the datastore behind a security group whose ingress names a security group the workload itself uses, and the units that exist only for a member and depend on it (volumes, autoscaling targets, the secret of a database, the roles and node security group of a cluster, the Service, Ingress, autoscaler, network policy and disruption budget of a Kubernetes workload). An application tag the source states as a literal (Application, App, ApplicationName, AppName, ApplicationId, Workload, or Service where there is none of those) names the application: workloads that share the value are one group, a tagged unit no workload reaches joins the group of its value, and a unit tagged with another value than the group that reaches it is shared. A tag read from a variable is shown and never decides. A unit that more than one group reaches is shared and belongs to no group, unless exactly one of them carries the unit's tag value. The network, the ECS cluster and the gateways belong to no group, and a module name never makes one. A group is named by its application tag, else by the name of its workload, else by the family of its task definition, else by its address.

https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/databases/postgresql-flex/how-tos/create-and-manage-instances-for-postgresql-flex/#instance-protection ("Instance Protection prevents an instance from being deleted. While it is active, deletion calls are rejected.") and the FAQ https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/databases/postgresql-flex/faq/ ("deleting an instance is immediate, permanent, and unrecoverable ... To prevent accidental deletion, enable Instance Protection."). The pages name the feature but not the tool that enables it: they do not state that Terraform supports it.

STACKIT provider schema 0.121.0 (the pinned provider version), re-read 2026-11-02: stackit_postgresflex_instance (attributes acl, backup_schedule, connection_info, encryption, flavor, flavor_id, id, instance_id, name, network, project_id, region, replicas, retention_days, storage, version) and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance (the same plus edition and options): no protection / deletable attribute, and no data source of the two services has one. The only attributes of the whole schema (resources and data sources) whose name contains protect, protection or deletable are protected (stackit_image, stackit_image_v2 and, new in 0.119.0, the results of the data source stackit_images: an image's protected flag), and protection (stackit_kms_key, stackit_kms_wrapping_key), all unrelated. The attribute sets of the two instance resources are the same as in the 0.116.0, 0.117.0 and 0.118.0 schemas (compared 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-10), and the STACKIT provider documentation of postgresflex_instance and sqlserverflex_instance (terraform-provider-stackit v0.116.0, local mirror) name no such attribute either. The fact holds on the pin: this refreshes the record of 2026-10-07, which cited the 0.117.0 schema and said that a 0.118.0 schema was not present, and was re-read on the 0.119.0 pin on 2026-10-10 (the 0.119.0 schema differs from 0.118.0 by two data sources and one resource description only) and again on the 0.120.0 pin on 2026-10-16 (the 0.120.0 schema differs from 0.119.0 by 17 block descriptions of the dremio, observability and secretsmanager services only, none of them a postgres/sqlserver flex type, an attribute or a type) and again on the 0.121.0 pin on 2026-11-02 (the 0.121.0 schema differs from 0.120.0 by one added attribute, config.cache_config of stackit_cdn_distribution, and one added data source, stackit_networks, found by a whole-tree comparison of the two files).

legs.source: STACKIT IaaS API v2 specification components.schemas.NIC.nicSecurity and CreateNicPayload.nicSecurity: "default": true, so a network interface created without nicSecurity has security (its security groups apply). NICSecurity: "If this is set to false, then no security groups will apply to this network interface."

https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/network/core-networking/network-interfaces/how-tos/create-and-manage-network-interfaces/ ("the optional flag `--nic-security` enables you to turn network interface security on. Per default it is disabled."), read 2026-10-08 through a page-summarising fetch tool. The sentence is about the CLI flag, not the API, so the two may both be true (the CLI would then send an explicit false); the page does not say. Probe 11: the page sentence is not true of STACKIT CLI 0.73.0 (its own help says "--nic-security ... (default true)", and `network-interface create` without the flag stored nicSecurity true), so the page is the outlier, not the specification.

STACKIT provider schema 0.121.0 resource_schemas.stackit_network_interface.block.attributes.security: optional, computed bool without a stated default; the provider (mirror tag v0.116.0, networkinterface/resource.go:643) sends nothing when it is unset, so the API default decides. Probe 11 (provider 0.118.0): a network interface written without security was stored and read back with nicSecurity true (state security = true). The attribute is the same in the 0.119.0 schema (re-read 2026-10-10) the 0.120.0 schema (re-read 2026-10-16) and the 0.121.0 schema (re-read 2026-11-02).

groups.message: The source restricts egress (the AWS provider removes AWS's default allow-all egress rule; only the listed egress rules apply). After apply, delete them (stackit security-group rule list / delete --security-group-id <id>), or egress is wider than in the source.

groups.message: At least one rule of this group is not in the draft as the source has it. The plan withholds it, holds it as a commented-out rule until a value or a decision is filled in, writes it with a fact that decides what it allows not carried exactly, or cannot name it at all because the source has more rules than are visible statically (a dynamic block over a collection, a count or a rule list that is not known until apply, or a list with a hidden member: the plan's INCOMPLETE action says which set and why, the draft's TODO "rules beyond the known set" names it, and only the known rules are drafted). Typical causes: a protocol, port or source whose value is known only at apply time or comes from a root variable; a source group that is a choice between groups or not a group of the draft; a protocol with no STACKIT counterpart; an ICMP type with every code; an ICMP or ICMPv6 rule whose range is of the other IP family (the API answers HTTP 400, the test of 2026-10-08); a tcp or udp rule with a negative port, a port above 65535, a reversed range, or port 0 only (STACKIT stores no port range for 0 to 0, so the rule would match every port). A tcp or udp range that starts at port 0 and ends below 65535 is written from port 1 (the STACKIT API rejects a range that starts at 0; tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-07): port 0 itself is not carried. A stackit_security_group_rule without protocol, port_range or source allows everything (the pinned STACKIT provider), so such a rule is never widened; re-create it with the values it needs (the plan names each one).

This route table is created with count or for_each. What the draft makes of it follows the decision of this unit. A table that STACKIT's default routing replaces (the cases of a table with only internet or NAT routes in a project outside a Network Area) is not drafted at all, whatever its count: no routing table is made and none is to be attached, and this warning only records that the table is repeated. A table the decision keeps as a routing table of its own (rt-custom) is made only where the source names, instance by instance, which route and which subnet belongs to which instance (a table created with count whose routes and associations name the table by their own count.index): one routing table for each instance, with the routes the draft carries in each, attached to no network, and none at all when the draft carries none of the routes. Where the source does not name them, the draft makes none (which instance a route belongs to is not decided). For a table the decision keeps, nothing in the draft states which VPC the table belonged to (the routing table the draft writes, stackit_routing_table, belongs to a Network Area; the experimental stackit_vpc_routing_table of the pinned provider takes a vpc_id, but the draft writes none): the table, its routes and the subnets it is associated with are re-created or attached by hand once the VPC architecture is decided.

groups.message: The project can be taken as one VPC's boundary only if every resource that names a VPC provably names the estate's one, and this estate does not show it: the VPC this subnet names, or the VPC another resource of the estate names (a network ACL, a flow log, a peering connection, a Cloud Control subnet, ...), is a literal id, a variable, a data source, an attribute of a VPC other than its id (its arn, its owner id, ...) or an expression the scan cannot reduce to one reference to the VPC the estate creates (or the estate creates no VPC of its own). A unit placed in a subnet that the scan cannot show is one of the estate's (a server, load balancer, function or NAT gateway in a subnet given by a variable, a data source or a literal id) is in the same position: it may stand in another VPC. The draft puts every network, security group and routing table in the one var.project_id and cannot say that they all belong to one VPC. Confirm which VPC each of them is in, and whether the networks of another VPC belong in this project or in a project of their own joined through a Network Area. No unit of the VPC topology is automation-eligible until then (gate blocker TOPOLOGY:vpc-unproven).
evidence: https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/network/core-networking/basics/architecture/

A state is read from a typed fact of the assessment or of a plan (an open critical semantic, an observed bootstrap, a source artifact the scan did not find, a manual action with its kind and phase); nothing is inferred from a resource name.
A compute unit is a unit of the catalogue category compute; every other unit applies to a dimension only where a typed fact concerns it.

The cutover requirement is read for the DNS records of this build only (the re-bound address of an Elastic IP, or an address record with no endpoint binding) and for the manual actions of the plan due before the cutover; the cutover of any other endpoint (load balancer, certificate, allow-list) is not read by this build. StackToIT applies no cutover and the requirement does not change a unit's class, confidence or eligibility.

options.name: Essential Support
includes: Free of charge and available to all STACKIT customers by default.
Ideal for development and test environments that host non-critical cloud workloads.
Service hours 10/5 for service requests, incidents and business-critical incidents.
Reaction time 15 minutes for all support cases; response time for business-critical incidents 4 hours; no response time targeted for service requests and other incidents (N/A).
caveats: The page states that, for Essential Support, these times are targeted on a best-effort basis, are not binding, and that exceeding them does not entitle the customer to penalties or financial compensation.
The page refers to sections A.5 and A.6 of the service description document for more information; that document was not read.

options.name: Advanced Support
includes: Designed for customers with cloud workloads that run in production and host business-critical services.
Booked on a per-project basis; can be cancelled monthly.
Service hours 10/5 for service requests and incidents; 24/7 for business-critical incidents.
Reaction time 15 minutes for all support cases; response time 8 hours for service requests, 4 hours for incidents, 1 hour for business-critical incidents.

supporting.detail: Product page (sales page: evidence that the plan is offered). Its footnote: "24/7 support refers exclusively to the response time for business-critical issues within the scope of STACKIT Advanced Support." Business-critical issues: 1 hour (24/7); incidents within 4 hours during business hours, Monday through Friday, 8:00-18:00.

caveats: 24/7 applies to business-critical incidents only; other incidents and service requests are handled in 10/5 hours.
The documents read do not say whether the stated times are contractual (SLA, penalties); the Advanced Support contract terms (Vertragsbedingungen) were not read.

options.name: Ultimate Support
includes: High-end support plan for enterprise customers who require immediate assistance for their most critical cloud workloads.

Reaction time 15 minutes for all support cases; response time 4 hours for service requests, 2 hours for incidents, 30 minutes for business-critical incidents.

supporting.detail: Product page (sales page: evidence that the features are offered). Lists 24/7 escalation management (an escalation manager can be activated 30 minutes after a business-critical ticket is opened), training and consulting, a dedicated number and service reports.

caveats: The documents read do not say whether the stated times are contractual (SLA, penalties); the Ultimate Support contract terms were not read.

limits: A list price is the price of one unit of one SKU. It is not a cost: this block reads no quantity and builds no total; the quantities, amounts and totals of the priced families are in financial/cost-model.json.

A resource is joined to a SKU only where the draft itself names the machine type, performance class or flavor; where the draft leaves that to a person (a variable), no SKU is named and the resource is NOT_ASSESSED.

Prices are net list prices of the public STACKIT price list: excluding taxes, with no contract discount, no savings plan and no other currency. A SKU that is not in the public list, a deprecated SKU and the metro variant of a SKU are never used as a price.
Egress and traffic, support plans, the container registry and every resource of a kind the price rules do not list have no row: nothing is stated about their cost.
Only the region eu01 is looked at: it is the region of the knowledge-base catalogue the draft takes its flavors from.
The row of a volume is the per-hour fee of its performance class; the capacity fee of the disk is a separate SKU that depends on the size, and is a line of the cost model, not a row here.

cost_model.statement: An initial infrastructure cost estimate under explicit assumptions (the scenario and the assumption file this model names), not a bill: list prices (net, no discount, no Spot, no savings plan, no private price) times quantities the source or the assumption file states. A total is FULL only when every line of its scope is priced; a line that cannot be priced says why and is never filled in, and an unknown quantity is neither 0 nor 1. A savings percentage is given only for the same scope, in one currency (or with an exchange rate that names its source and date), with every line of both sides priced. No usage, traffic, request, egress, support or one-off migration cost is computed.

NAT gateway: the hour of a zonal public NAT gateway is priced and the data it processes has the per-GB price and no quantity; the STACKIT price list holds no SKU for a NAT gateway or for outbound address translation, so its target line is PRICE_NOT_FOUND (a service the list does not price is not free). Load balancer: the hour of an Application or Network Load Balancer is priced and its capacity units have the price and no quantity; the target line is the hour of the plan (plan_id; a Network Load Balancer that states none is read as the default p10 the provider documents). Public IPv4 address: the hour of an Elastic IP, and of the address an instance asks for with associate_public_ip_address = true (not an address its subnet or launch template decides), against the hour of a stackit_public_ip. DNS: the month of a hosted zone (the first tier of the Route 53 price; the tier is the account's) and its queries (no quantity); the STACKIT list prices a zone by the number of records it may hold, which the draft does not state, so its target line is AMBIGUOUS. Data transfer out: the per-GB price of the first tier (every tier is named on the line) on the line of the internet gateway and no quantity; the STACKIT list holds no SKU for it, so its target line is PRICE_NOT_FOUND. A quantity that is a measurement of use (GB, capacity unit hours, queries) is never in a Terraform source and is never made up: such a line has its price and no amount. The prices are the On-Demand rows of the AmazonEC2 (NAT gateway, load balancers), AmazonVPC (public IPv4), AWSDataTransfer and AmazonRoute53 offers of the price cache, which `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws --region R` fetches (`--offer` names one); a line whose offer the cache does not hold names the offer and the command.

The managed-service families are priced from the On-Demand rows of the AmazonECS (Fargate vCPU and GB hours: the cpu and memory of the task definition times the desired count, which is never taken as zero when it is not stated), AmazonMQ (broker hour by engine, instance type and deployment mode; its storage has the price and no quantity), AmazonElastiCache (node hour by engine and node type times the nodes of a replication group), AmazonES (data and dedicated master node hours, EBS GB-month) and AmazonDynamoDB (provisioned read and write capacity unit hours when the table states them, at the rate beyond the free first tier, which is the whole account's; request units and storage have the price and no quantity) offers, which `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws --region R` fetches (`--offer` names one); Fargate Spot, ECS on EC2 capacity, Windows tasks, global datastores and non-standard table classes are out of the model. On the target side a RabbitMQ, Valkey (Key Value Store), OpenSearch or MariaDB instance is the hour of the SKU of its plan_name (the SKU is named by the plan, INFERRED from the names of the list, and its nodes and disk are checked against the list's attributes); a plan the draft leaves to a person is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN. An SKE cluster is the cluster hour, and each node pool it states is a line of its own: the server flavor hours of its machine_type (the join of a server) times its nodes, the range between its minimum and its maximum when they differ, an unknown quantity with the price when the draft states either as a variable, and TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN when the machine type is a variable; the boot volume of each node is not in the line, and the nodes of an EKS node group or of an ECS cluster's capacity have no source line in this build, so a pool is a target-only line (see below). A MongoDB Flex instance is the hour of the SKU MongoDB-Flex-<cpu>.<ram>-<Single|Replica|Sharded> of its flavor.cpu, flavor.ram and options.type (INFERRED from the names of the list, and checked against the SKU's own attributes; the rate of a Replica SKU is read as that of the whole instance with its nodes); a flavor a person sets is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN, a flavor the list has no SKU of is PRICE_NOT_FOUND, its storage and backups are not computed, and because this build prices no DocumentDB cluster on the source side its line is target only (see below). A software KMS key version and a GB of log ingestion have their list price and no quantity; Secrets Manager is AMBIGUOUS between its tiers (the number of secret versions). A priced target line of a family whose source side has no line for the unit (an SKE cluster and its node pools, a MariaDB instance, a MongoDB Flex instance, a RabbitMQ plan against a source with no priced broker) is target only: it is counted in the STACKIT total, listed apart with its amount (target_only on the line and target_only_lines, target_only_min and target_only_max on the total), and kept out of every comparison and every saving, because no source amount stands against it; each comparison states the lines and the amount it leaves out, on both sides.

The instance hours and the allocated storage of an RDS for PostgreSQL instance are priced from the AmazonRDS offer of the price cache (On-Demand list prices, Single-AZ or Multi-AZ as the source states; `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws` fetches it with the AmazonEC2 offer); its provisioned IOPS (io1, io2, gp3) and the provisioned throughput of gp3 storage come from the same offer, gp3 only above the performance its allocated storage includes (a baseline of 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s from 400 GiB, nothing more can be provisioned below it: Amazon RDS User Guide, DB instance storage); without that offer the lines are PRICE_SOURCE_ABSENT and the instance is never in the computed subtotal. An Aurora instance (engine aurora-mysql or aurora-postgresql) is the instance hour of its engine, its instance class and the storage configuration of its cluster, from the same offer (rules version 3 of its narrowing): Aurora Standard when the cluster states no storage_type (the provider's documented default), Aurora I/O-Optimized for storage_type = "aurora-iopt1", and both prices open (AMBIGUOUS) when the source does not state it as a fact or the instance's cluster is not a resource of the source; the cluster's consumed storage (a GB-month) and, on Standard, its I/O requests are measurements of use and have their price and no quantity. An Aurora Serverless v2 instance (db.serverless), an instance of a Multi-AZ DB cluster, backup storage beyond the free allocation, Global Database and the Data API are not computed. An offer narrowed before the Aurora rows were kept answers PRICE_SOURCE_ABSENT with the refresh command on each Aurora line. A PostgreSQL Flex Replica flavor is priced once per instance: the list gives its SKU 3 nodes and a higher rate than the Single SKU (1.6 to 2.0 times it, never 3 times), and the rate is read as that of the whole instance (evidence class INFERRED from the price list; each such line says so); how much of its storage is billed (once or per node) the list does not say, so its storage lines have the SKU and no quantity.

The PostgreSQL Flex storage class premium-perf<n>-stackit is priced as the SKU "Block Storage for PostgreSQL Premium-Performance <n>" per disk and its capacity as "Block Storage for PostgreSQL Premium-Capacity" per GB (evidence class INFERRED from the names of the price list; each such line says so). The IOPS and throughput shown for the class in the technical mapping are the attributes maxIOPerSec and maxTroughInMB of that performance SKU in the price list (the catalogue states none for a PostgreSQL Flex class); whether the class covers what the source provisions is a comparison of those figures, not a statement that the two perform alike.

The lines fall into three groups: the computed subtotal (only the source units every line of which is priced on both sides, so both subtotals cover the same units), the lines whose price is known and whose quantity is not (the quantity that is needed is named), and what is not computed (a unit of a type out of the model, a unit with no line on one side, or a line without a price), listed by resource and never zero.

Source prices are the On-Demand list prices of the AWS offer file in the price cache (USD, net, region of the resource); Spot, Reserved, Savings Plans, Dedicated Host, capacity reservation and private prices are never used. The operating system and licence come from the assumption file: the source does not state them.

The offer file bills an EBS volume per GB-month; this build reads it as GiB-month, the unit a volume is sized in: the Amazon EBS pricing page states "on this page, GB = 1024^3 bytes" (OFFICIAL_DOCUMENTED for that page; applying it to the offer file's unit is INFERRED). The IOPS and throughput of a gp3 volume are priced only above the baseline included in the price of its storage (3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s: Amazon EBS User Guide, OFFICIAL_DOCUMENTED), per volume; io2 IOPS are priced in tiers whose edges the offer file carries in descriptions only, and are not priced.

Target prices are the net EUR list prices of the public STACKIT price list in the price cache (region eu01). A machine type or performance class the draft leaves to a person is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN; the metro variant of a SKU is never substituted.
The target capacity price of a volume is the capacity SKU of its performance class's tier (evidence class INFERRED from the structure of the price list).

One month is the 730 hours of the scenario; a per-month rate is applied as the file gives it. Snapshots, backups, support plans and every other cost of usage, traffic or requests that this build has no line for are not computed.
A saving is compared only for the same source units on both sides and in one currency (an exchange rate from the assumption file, with its source and date, converts one side).

machine_files.description: The full assessment: every unit, finding and count, machine-readable. Every number in this workspace is read from it.
The assessment in words: the run status and its checks, and for each unit the class, the confidence and the STACKIT target proposed.
The working behind engineering/architect-report.md: the relations and combinations the engine evaluated for the decisions that depend on them. Nothing here is a second decision.
The source and the target architecture as a diagram in Mermaid text, for tools that draw it. The Architecture section of this page draws the same units itself.
A draft order of work: waves computed from the dependencies between units. A starting point for the architect's plan, not a schedule.
One row per unit for spreadsheet review.
One row per dependency between units, for the architect to confirm, correct or complete.
The compact model the pages show, machine-readable. No page embeds it: the pages are complete without it, and a tool reads the model from this file.
The front page: the header, the navigation and the Overview. The other sections are the pages in pages/.
The Applications section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Which application each unit belongs to, and each application's migration strategy.
The Architecture section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The units of the estate and what the assessment decided for each.
The Decisions section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The decisions people must take, aggregated, with their options, owners and deadlines.

The Target Fit section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. How well each STACKIT target fits: service, interface, Terraform, region, maturity, quota, lifecycle, operability, support and security.
The Migration Plan section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Waves, prerequisites, data movement and the order of work.

The Security & Resilience section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. What has been proven about security and resilience, what has not, and what needs evidence from outside; the resilience of each unit, where this run assesses it, is on the Operations page.
The Sovereignty section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Dependencies, jurisdiction, data placement, key control and exit paths, source against target.
The Operations section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Whether the target can be run: identity, audit, observability, backup, restore, support and lifecycle.
The Costs section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Priced and unpriced coverage, and the inputs a cost estimate needs.
The Evidence section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The counts, versions and sources behind every statement in this workspace.
The Engineering Evidence section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The machine-readable files and the Terraform draft.

The Work Board section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Every job of the migration in one list, in four queues: who does it, what it waits for, what closes it and which file it carries out.

The group pages of the Decisions section: the full cards of the records the page does not hold, one page per work package (the page of the section lists the groups), and, for a very large estate, its long lists cut into pages of a size a browser opens. Present only when the register has more records than the page holds cards.
The decision register, machine-readable, with a template of the decisions file to fill in.
The decision records as rows for a spreadsheet.
The decision records in words.

The five-minute answer as a document: the run summary, what holds the estate back, what people must decide, the shape of the target and what has and has not been established. It restates numbers this file holds and scores nothing.

One row per application of the applications file you gave, with the values as you wrote them (a value you did not write is marked not provided), and one row per unit claimed by several applications. Header only without an applications file.

The dependency order of the units, one row per unit: the wave, WITHHELD when a part of the source was not read in full, or REFUSED for a unit the partial draft refuses for a missing input (in no wave). An order of work, not a schedule.

The register of what a person has to do, decide or establish before the draft is deployed, one typed row per item: gaps in the reading of the source, critical semantics left open, open decisions and manual actions of the plans, workload items that wait for evidence, and validation rows not yet established. Every member of decisions.json is a row; each row names the decision record that holds it. It lists what is open and decides nothing.

The Work Board as a sheet: one row per job of the migration, in one of four queues (provide information, approve a design, perform migration work, verify), with its owner, priority, what it waits for, what closes it, its evidence, the files it carries out and the steps of the execution plan it holds. Every step of the plan is in exactly one job, or listed as not taken; pages/work-board.html shows the same jobs. Header only when the run wrote no execution plan.

Each source unit beside its STACKIT target, one row per unit: the target service and its resources, or in words that there is none, that the unit is refused or that the source switches it off, and how many of its settings are kept (PRESERVED), changed (TRANSFORMED), accepted (ACCEPTED_*) or still to do (everything else, including anything not known). Counted from the rows of assurance/equivalence-ledger.csv; a unit with no ledger row has four zeros, which says nothing was counted, not that nothing is left to do. Header only when the Workspace holds no counts.

The drill-down from each application of the customer's file and each group the run suggested (PROPOSED: a reading of the source, not confirmed by anyone), one row per member unit: the AWS resource, the STACKIT target in the words of migration/source-target.csv, the ids of the decisions that still ask something about the unit, the steps of the execution plan that carry it with the number an answer leaves not taken, the Kubernetes manifest objects that tie to it by an exact literal match, and what the code scan says of the application. A run that read no plan or built no register marks those cells as not assessed, which is not an empty list. Header only when the Workspace holds none.
For each unit, the open decisions and manual actions that stand between its draft and its deployment, as its plan states them.

One row per stateful source unit (a database, a cache, a volume, a file share, an object store): its source and target service, the data class, RPO and downtime tolerance you stated (or marked not provided), the provisioned capacity the source states (not the size of the data) and the cutover dependency. The mechanism of every unit is UNKNOWN: StackToIT never moves data.
The same units in words, with what the source and the plans do and do not state about each. No size, change rate, duration, transfer rate or downtime is ever stated, and no mechanism is chosen.

The data_movement block of workspace.json with every stateful source unit (the facets, the unknowns, the provisioned capacity and where each fact is read from), as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to. workspace.json carries the tally of the units.
The units of the estate and the dependencies among them as a Mermaid flowchart, with the units of each application drawn together.
The same units with the STACKIT service proposed for each, its class and confidence, as a Mermaid flowchart.
The same units with what the move changes for each: its class, whether it has a target, and how many properties the draft names as not carried.
The drawing of the source architecture of the Architecture section, as a file of its own, without the links of the page.
The drawing of the proposed STACKIT target of the Architecture section, as a file of its own.
The drawing of what the move changes, as a file of its own.
What has and has not been established about the draft, row by row, with the global invariants. It approves nothing and asserts neither equivalence nor that the draft is safe to apply.
How much of the source was read, the source providers the assessment saw and the source types the knowledge base does not know.
How the STACKIT targets of the units stand in the capability catalogue and in the pinned provider (maturity, lifecycle), and the readiness dimensions.
The workload readiness of the units (installation, source artifacts, target preconditions, cutover, day 2) and the support options STACKIT evidences. Terraform generated is not workload ready.
For each STACKIT service of the draft and each framework in scope, the state of the provider's own evidence. It says nothing about the compliance of your workload.
The cells of compliance-evidence.md as rows for a spreadsheet.

The equivalence ledger: one row per unit and semantic of the assessment that the source states (workspace.json counts those it does not state), and one row per unit and property for the properties the draft does not carry, no semantic accounts for or that are critical and still open. Each row says how the source states the value, what proves the disposition, where the draft carries it and what stays open. Dispositions are the words the assessment uses today; PRESERVED appears only where the assessment or the draft's plan states it.

The evidence the ledger and the other blocks cite, one row per document, with what it backs, the date it was checked, the date after which it is to be checked again and its state. Evidence that states no such dates is UNDATED, never CURRENT.

The open critical semantics, one row per unit and semantic, with the disposition the contract result gives, the cause code, the sentences that say why the semantic is open and what would close it, the instances of a repeated unit and the alarm card where there is one. These are the rows the decision records name as their members; workspace.json carries the tally of them, with the run it belongs to.

The RTO and RPO you stated (or that none was stated) and, for each unit that holds state or states a zone, replication or backup fact, what the source states. No unit is called resilient and no intent is chosen.

The resilience block of workspace.json with every unit that states a failure-domain, replication or backup fact or holds state (the quoted source facts, the state and where each fact is read from), as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to. workspace.json carries the tally of the units.

For each unit that runs as an identity or is one: the identities the source names, the static credential the knowledge base reads, the federation facts, the attachment the identity plan holds and its state. It makes no claim that federation is an option; privilege delta, break-glass access and human identity are not assessed.

The sovereignty requirement (not provided unless your applications file states one), the dimensions of sovereignty with what the source shows and what the target is proposed to be, the dependencies and the exitability. Sovereignty is not residency; it holds no score and certifies no legal compliance.
The sovereignty block of workspace.json as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to.

The price_snapshot block of workspace.json as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to: which snapshot of the public STACKIT price list this run cites (source, retrieval date, sha256, currency, net list price) and how many of the drafted resources it priced. It holds list prices only: no quantity is read, no total is built, and no usage and no egress is computed.

The cost model of the run, line by line: for each component of the AWS source (EC2 instances and EBS volumes) and of the STACKIT target (servers and volumes) its quantity (a value, a range or unknown, and where it comes from), its price record or the reason there is none, its pricing state and its amount; then the totals of the estate and of each service for each side (full, partial or none), the comparison of source and target with the reason a saving is or is not given, the price sources (the local price cache) and the assumptions the figures rest on. An estimate under one labelled scenario, not a bill.

One row for each line of the cost model (financial/cost-model.json), source and target: the quantity with its provenance, the price record (SKU, rate, unit, the date it is valid from, the snapshot it comes from) or the state and the reason there is none, and the amount of a priced line. An empty amount is a line that is not priced, never a zero.

The technical mapping beside the prices: for each server, boot disk, disk and database whose source and target are both in the computed group of the cost model, what each side states about vCPU, memory, CPU model, disk capacity, IOPS, throughput and high availability. The source side is read from the attributes of the source resource, the target side from the catalogue snapshot of the region; a fact a side does not state is the words not stated. A machine type is one of the types of the catalogue with at least the vCPUs and memory of the source (a burstable source may be offered shared types); a storage class is the one the draft names (the customer's answer or the variable's default), shown with the catalogue's own IOPS and throughput. The table states sizes; it is not a statement about the performance of the target against the source (no benchmark was run, and a CPU model that a side does not state is shown as not stated). The last six columns add, for a disk, the fee of the selected performance class (the cost model's own amount) with the assumption behind the class, whether the class covers the IOPS and throughput of the source volume, and the smaller classes of the catalogue that still cover them with their fee and change (an alternative with the same or better figures than the source; not a recommendation), and, for a server, whether the flavor is with or without CPU overprovisioning (the documentation's terms, by the overcommit the catalogue states) and what STACKIT states of its lifecycle (a deprecated type says so, with the sentence of the documentation). The size match columns state the comparison of a server's machine type with the source instance and of a database's PostgreSQL Flex flavor with the RDS instance class (vCPUs, memory and the kind, single node or replica set, against Multi-AZ) as proven, to review, not met or unknown, with the sentence that says what was compared; a basis names a size only where the size match is proven.

What the cost model covers: the price sources it looked at, the lines by pricing state for each side, the totals with their state (full, partial or none), the comparison of source and target and why a saving is or is not given, the assumptions, and what the list prices of the STACKIT snapshot cover, with what is known of the terms of reuse of the price data.

One row per property the draft names as not carried: the unit, the node and the property, what the assessment states about it (the class and closure of the critical-property gate, the draft's own reason, the contract semantic that reads it, what closes that semantic while it is open) and the place of the node in the source. A cell the assessment states nothing for is empty.
The units for which the draft names properties as not carried, with how many, and the units that have no count (their draft block was not accounted, or they need no resource of their own).

The reverse table of the evidence index: one entry per block of the draft, with the units it comes from, whether it is an HCL block, a comment or not placed, and its file and line, with the hop table and the checks over the draft. workspace.json carries the tally of the entries and, on each unit, the forward hops; this file is the mirror of them, with the run it belongs to.

The full comment of each block of the Terraform draft that has one: the draft keeps a one-paragraph comment above the block (where it comes from, why its values are what they are, what is not carried, which decision is open) and a `# trace: TR-...` line, and the section of this folder that line names holds the whole comment the generators wrote, unabridged: the rule and knowledge-base stamp, the references with their digests, the evidence of each chosen value and the reason of each attribute that is not written. One file for each file of the draft that has such a block, named after it with the extension .md, one section for each block under an anchor that is its trace id; the blocks are linked to their file by `trace_file` and their anchor `trace_id` in engineering/evidence-index.json. This run wrote 8 files with 48 sections.

One row per block with a trace: the trace id, the block, the draft file, the source units, the lines of the comment as the generators wrote it and the lines the draft keeps, and the pointer of the block (the trace file and the anchor of its section).

The input variables of the draft: the values a person fills in.

The canonical TargetPlans the draft was generated from, machine-readable: one plan for each family of the draft that is written from a plan (the security groups of each source cloud, routing, identity, log sources, servers), each with how the draft wrote every resource of it (a resource, a comment only, or a statement about a block another generator writes). The run read it back against the draft before it was published: every resource of a plan is, or is not, a block of the draft as the file says. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The execution package: execution/README.md is the entry point for carrying the migration out (the verdict for the resources with a typed plan and the draft files it does not cover, what is created, what is not migrated, the decisions, the credentials, the order of the steps, the OpenTofu and API commands, the manual steps, the checks and the rollback); execution/terraform/apply.md, one request file and one script per STACKIT API call under execution/api/, execution/manual/actions.md and execution/verify/checks.md beside it. A rendering of execution-plan.json and of nothing else; nothing in it has been run, and a script stops before it calls anything when its step waits for a decision. Present only when the run produced the draft.

One row per step of execution-plan.json for a spreadsheet: id, phase, mode, source, target, dependencies, owner, status, file, risks, rollback, whether it is executable and the decisions it waits for. The steps to carry out, not the register of open items (migration/actions.csv). Present only when the run produced the draft.

One row per work package of the manual steps of execution-plan.json for a spreadsheet: the steps of one phase, one owner role and one kind of work that one person carries out together, with their number, the resources they touch, the decisions they rest on and wait for, the strictest state among them, their success conditions and the ids of the steps. Every manual step is in exactly one package; execution/README.md lists the same packages. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The network and security view as a Mermaid flowchart, or, in an estate with more than 120 units in it, the partition map of the files under architecture/partitions/ (one box for each partition, the arrows between partitions counted, every unknown edge accounted for). Drawn from the TargetPlans of the draft and the assessment: the internet, public IPs, load balancers, networks, subnets, servers, databases, security groups and their rules, network ACLs and routing. A path the sources do not state is a dashed edge labelled unknown with its reason, never a connection that was not read. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The identity view as a Mermaid flowchart (an estate with more principals than a drawing keeps legible gets one sentence that names assurance/identity-transition.md, which lists every identity, instead of a drawing): the AWS principal, the decision the assessment and the plan hold for it, the STACKIT identity it moves to, the role assignment and its scope. A step the typed plan does not hold (the role assignment) is drawn as manual, and a step it leaves open is a dashed edge labelled unknown. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The data flows as a Mermaid flowchart, or, in an estate with more than 120 units in it, the partition map of the files under architecture/partitions/ (one box for each partition, the arrows between partitions counted, every unknown edge accounted for): clients, load balancers, applications, databases, object storage and registries, with the protocol and port of each flow where the source states them, public or private, and the migration effect on the unit that carries it; what the source does not state is written unknown. The flows are the paths the listeners and security group rules permit, not observed traffic. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The network and security view drawn offline: the same boxes and arrows as architecture/network-security.mmd, each arrow numbered, with a key that gives its two ends in the direction of the arrow and its words (protocol, port and direction of a rule; the attribute of a reference). Source links, target links (what a rule, route or listener of the draft permits), links an answer of the inputs file changed and unknowns are drawn apart and named in the legend. A view that is not drawn whole (a partition map above 120 units) is one sentence. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The data flow view drawn offline: the same boxes and arrows as architecture/data-flows.mmd, each flow numbered, with a key that gives its two ends in the direction of the flow, its protocol and port, public or private, and the migration effect. Source links, target links and unknowns are drawn apart and named in the legend. A view that is not drawn whole (a partition map above 120 units) is one sentence. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The execution plan laid out in ten waves: wave 0 the decisions some step waits for, then the landing zone, network and security, data services, platform, workloads, data migration, cutover, verification and decommission. Each step names what it does, the AWS resource, the mode, what it depends on and whether it is ready, blocked by a decision, not ready or refused. It holds the steps of execution-plan.json only. Present only when the run produced the draft.
